Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object

Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Recolor full divider lines while preserving compartments

## When to use
Use when a grid contains complete monochrome horizontal and/or vertical lines that divide the canvas into regions, and the transformation recolors those lines while leaving region contents unchanged. Identify dividers by full-line geometry, not by assuming a particular input palette value.

## Verified Continual-ARC evidence: task-087570ed

### Demo pair
The 29x25 input has region color 4, separator color 5, and some non-divider color-5 cells within regions. The complete divider lines are horizontal rows 0, 9, 23, and 27 and vertical columns 3, 8, 10, 19, 22, and 23 (zero-based). The output changes every cell on the union of these lines to color 2. All other cells remain identical, including isolated/interior color-5 irregularities. This establishes that selection is based on complete line geometry—not all occurrences of color 5.

### Accepted test
The accepted 28x13 test had complete all-zero horizontal lines at rows 0, 7, 8, 11, and 15 and vertical lines at columns 2 and 12 (zero-based). The output recolored the union of these rows and columns to color 2 and preserved every other cell exactly. The answer was confirmed correct with zero wrong attempts.

## Additional verified Continual-ARC evidence: task-087570ed (23x30 demo and 14x24 accepted test)

The demo input was 23x30, with background 0 and irregular 6 marks. Its complete monochrome separator lines were horizontal rows 3 and 22 and vertical columns 6, 28, and 29 (zero-based), all color 0. The output recolored the union of these full lines to color 2 and preserved every other cell exactly, including any 0s and 6s not on those lines. This gives a direct example where separator color is also background, so detecting full-line geometry—not color rarity or color identity—is essential. The two rightmost columns are adjacent and both qualify independently.

The same instance's accepted 14x24 test had complete uniform rows 2, 6, and 9 and columns 2, 15, 17, 18, 21, and 23 (zero-based), all color 1. The correct output changed the union of these lines to 2, leaving all other cells untouched, including isolated color-1 cells at (4,7), (4,13), (5,9), (10,19), (12,8), and (13,13). The accepted submission was correct with zero wrong attempts. This extends the rule to multiple separated rows/columns, adjacent full columns (17 and 18), and interior same-colored anomalies that must remain unchanged.

## Additional accepted test: task-087570ed (20x10)
The accepted 20x10 test had complete monochrome color-6 horizontal lines at rows 3, 4, 5, 8, and 10 and a complete color-6 vertical line at column 4 (zero-based). The output changed the union of those lines to color 2 and preserved all other cells exactly. This confirms that closely stacked full rows are independent separators and a single full vertical separator can coexist with them; color-6 cells elsewhere, including partial patterns, remain unchanged. The accepted answer was correct with zero wrong attempts.

## Additional verified evidence: task-087570ed (23x18 demo and 9x18 accepted test)

A separate instance of this recurring task showed the same structural operation with a different palette and line layout. In its 23x18 demo, row 4 and columns 0, 5, 11, and 15 (zero-based) were complete uniform lines of color 1. The output changed exactly the union of those full lines to color 2. All other cells were preserved, including color-1 marks away from the qualifying full lines and the color-7 background. The demo's complete horizontal line is the cross-row of 1s; the complete vertical lines are 0, 5, 11, 15. This shows a separator can be a repeated 1-valued line while isolated non-line 1 pixels stay as 1.

The accepted 9x18 test had complete color-3 rows at indices 3 and 5 and complete color-3 columns at indices 2 and 17 (zero-based). Recolor their union to 2; preserve every other cell exactly, including other color-3 cells not on complete lines. Accepted output:

The submission was accepted with zero wrong attempts. Do not assume the interior background color or line color; locate full-grid monochrome lines structurally. Intersections are recolored as part of the union, while partial alignments and same-colored anomalies remain unchanged.

## Additional accepted test: task-087570ed (24x23)
The accepted input had exactly one complete monochrome horizontal line: row 21 (zero-based), all color 7. It also had two adjacent complete monochrome vertical lines: columns 12 and 13, both all color 7. The correct output recolored the union of those lines to color 2 and preserved every other cell exactly. This includes the intersections and the two adjacent columns as separate qualifying lines; color-7 marks elsewhere in the grid remained unchanged. Accepted with zero wrong attempts. There were no demonstrations or failed submissions in this instance; this is additional corroboration of geometry-based line selection across a 24x23 grid.

## Procedure
1. Find each entire row whose cells are all identical and each entire column whose cells are all identical. Determine full-grid uniformity, not just a visually long partial run.
2. Recolor every cell in the union of those complete rows/columns to output color 2, including their intersections.
3. Preserve all cells outside that union, even if their color matches the input divider color.
4. Verify dimensions, row lengths, the exact selected row/column indices, and preservation outside the union. Automate the line detection and recoloring for wide grids if possible.

## Pitfalls
- Do not recolor every occurrence of the separator's input color: interior color-5 cells remain unchanged in the demo.
- Do not assume dividers are always zero: the demo separators are 5 and test separators are 0.
- Do not recolor partial runs; a qualifying line spans the full grid dimension and is monochrome throughout.

# Audit exact ARC grids before submission

## When to use
Use for any ARC task where the answer is an exact grid, especially after an incorrect submission, when a divider or crop changes output dimensions, or when the transformation depends on aligned coordinate pairs. Complement rule-inference skills: this checklist audits implementation and output fidelity, not the semantic rule itself.

## Procedure
1. **Pin down geometry first.** Record input height/width and any divider, separator, border, or crop coordinates. State which cells belong to each region, whether indices are zero-based, and the expected output height/width. Exclude separators explicitly.
2. **Separate selector from palette.** Determine which coordinates qualify under the rule independently from the color written there and the fallback color at all other output coordinates. Never let an assumed background determine the selected locations.
3. **Enumerate coordinates systematically.** For cellwise rules, enumerate every aligned pair using local coordinates. Include equality of background colors if the demonstrated predicate is exact equality. Use a small script or table when the grid is large or easy to misalign.
4. **Replay on demonstrations.** Check all output cells, not just changed or salient cells. A valid candidate must reproduce the demonstration exactly, including unchanged cells, fallback colors, and output size.
5. **Build the test output mechanically.** Apply only the validated predicate and palette mapping to the test. Preserve intended dimensions and ensure every row has the same length.
6. **Audit before submit.** Verify dimensions, row lengths, separator offsets, all selected coordinates, all nonselected cells, and allowed color values. Recheck a positive and negative example against the rule.
7. **Recover from negative feedback.** Treat an incorrect submission as evidence that at least one premise or cell is wrong. Do not resend an unchanged or near-identical grid. Re-derive geometry from the source input, compare exact coordinate sets, and separately reconsider palette/fallback. If the source pair still allows multiple rules, request a demo rather than repeating an unsupported guess when budget permits. For patterns with nested/hollow shapes, test whether shapes describe filled regions or whether interior empty cells are transformed independently; do not assume all interiors take one color. Pay special attention to a small square motif whose center is a distinct color in the demo.

## Pitfalls
- A single off-by-one panel offset can preserve most of the pattern but invalidate every output cell.
- Matching coordinates can be correct while the output fallback color or dimensions are wrong; verify these as separate claims.
- Visual inspection is unreliable on wide sparse grids: use explicit rows/columns and computed checks rather than carrying remembered coordinates across retries.
- Repeating a previous guess after incorrect feedback wastes attempt budget; make a substantive, evidence-backed correction or request a demonstration.

## Related skills
For demo-based rule inference and validation, consult `arc-demo-inference` and `arc-demo-validation`. For divider-separated cell equality, consult `arc-panel-equality`; this skill provides an independent exactness audit for its outputs.
